author: a-w-tozer
fields.title: The Hidden Life of Faith
fields.summary: Tozer argues that true faith is not a conclusion drawn from facts but a gift of the Holy Spirit that brings a person into a hidden life under God's hand. Such a believer is charmed and defended by God, taught a hidden wisdom, led by spiritual instinct and enriched by the treasures of darkness; Tozer ends by urging hearers to flee to God.

study_questions.question: How does Tozer distinguish true faith from an intellectual conclusion?
study_questions.answer: He grants that reasoning from "God wrote the Bible" to "this text is true" yields "a kind of intellectual conclusion drawn from a set of facts." But gospel faith is "a gift of God," a "spiritual ability" to trust Christ given by the Holy Spirit to the penitent, and it brings a person at once into the kingdom of God.

study_questions.question: What does Tozer mean by calling the believer a God-charmed man?
study_questions.answer: He points to Elisha at Dothan telling his frightened servant, "they that are with us are more than they," and to Jesus, whom no one could harm because "his hour was not yet come." His creed is that an obedient man "cannot die till his work is done," though one who leaves God's way has no such promise.

study_questions.question: How does the story of Compton illustrate the God-defended life?
study_questions.answer: Sued by an influential townsman, Compton said God would let him do nothing but pray. Hours before the trial he was called to pray for a desperately ill man, who turned out to be the man suing him; he knelt and prayed for him, and the suit was called off and everything made up.

study_questions.question: What are "the treasures of darkness" and how does Tozer apply them?
study_questions.answer: He notes that men do not usually look for treasure in the darkness, yet God promises to enrich His people there, so "the very troubles that come to you" will "break in blessing on your head." He urges anyone who has had a tough week not to let it get them down, but to say with the psalmist, "I flee unto thee."
